profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a global financial research and advisory firm preparing a client-facing rollout for a new thought-leadership piece titled "On the Normality of Negative Interest Rates." The piece will be distributed to bank treasury clients as a short white paper, accompanied by a slide deck, a webinar, and a sales briefing note. The meeting is between the research lead and the capital-markets content operations manager to align on handoffs between the economics workstream and the publishing/distribution workstream. The agenda is to confirm what version of the paper is considered ready for downstream use, what materials are included in the "client pack," what it means for the piece to be "signed off," and how the Thursday delivery date should be interpreted across teams in London and New York. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on timeline, ownership, and deliverables so the publishing team can proceed without escalating questions.

members.name: Elena Markovic
members.expertise: Monetary economics, policy analysis, central-bank communication, research drafting
members.background: Elena leads the firm's macro thought-leadership program and previously worked as an economist at a European central bank; she is used to circulating near-final drafts internally before polishing language late in the process.
members.private_state: She wants the distribution team to start building around the paper now so the publication lands before an upcoming client roundtable, but she also expects to keep making small editorial and chart changes up to the last minute and wants to avoid a lengthy approval loop with Legal unless absolutely necessary.
hidden_assumptions: "Final draft" means the argument, structure, and exhibits are stable enough for dependent teams to build slides and summaries, even if wording, chart labels, and disclaimer placement may still change.
"Signed off" for a research note means approval from her and the Chief Economist; Legal only needs to review the external email copy, not the paper PDF itself, unless it contains product advice.
"Client pack" naturally refers to the white paper PDF plus the webinar deck outline; the sales one-pager and talking points are separate downstream enablement items owned by distribution.
A Thursday delivery promise refers to end of business in London because the research team publishes on London market cadence.
When people refer to "the reserve-rate chart," they mean the updated simulation figure with the CBDC lower-bound scenario that replaced the earlier cash-bound chart in her working folder.

members.name: Jason Reed
members.expertise: Publication workflows, cross-regional scheduling, client distribution, compliance handoffs
members.background: Jason coordinates external release packages across research, design, compliance, and sales enablement; he previously worked in investor communications at a U.S. asset manager where document freezes and package completeness were tightly managed.
members.private_state: He wants a clean handoff that can move through design, compliance tagging, CRM upload, and regional distribution without rework, and he is trying to prevent another last-minute scramble caused by research changing files after operations has already scheduled sends.
hidden_assumptions: "Final draft" means file-locked content that will not materially change after design begins, except perhaps for typo fixes.
"Signed off" for anything going to clients includes Compliance/Legal approval of the PDF, deck, and summary note before scheduling.
"Client pack" normally includes every item a relationship manager will receive or forward: the PDF, slide deck, webinar invite copy, and a one-page sales brief with approved talking points.
A Thursday delivery promise means by 5 p.m. New York time because distribution and CRM scheduling are run from the U.S. operations queue.

When people refer to "the reserve-rate chart," they mean the previously circulated Figure 4 showing the cash lower-bound constraint, because that is the version already sent to design for layout testing.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the final draft
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the paper as the "final draft" that can be handed off on Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena means a substantively complete draft whose thesis and figures are stable enough for downstream teams to proceed, while she still expects to edit prose, chart annotations, and framing language afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jason means the file is frozen for production and can enter design, compliance tagging, and upload with no meaningful changes afterward.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research publishing, "final draft" sounds like a routine milestone both teams use constantly; each assumes the other shares the industry's obvious meaning from their own workflow, so the term creates false consensus without inviting clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Jason will prepare the "client pack" once research sends materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena thinks the client pack covers the core research assets needed for publication: the paper PDF and the webinar deck skeleton based on the paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jason thinks the client pack includes all downstream client-facing collateral: PDF, deck, webinar copy, approved sales brief, and talking points for relationship managers.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sides use the same packaging term from previous launches, and because each item sounds like a natural extension of the same release, neither pauses to enumerate contents during a quick coordination call.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the piece just needs to be "signed off" before Jason schedules distribution.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena believes sign-off is achieved once she and the Chief Economist approve the intellectual content, since the note is policy analysis rather than product commentary.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jason believes sign-off means all required internal approvals, including Compliance/Legal review for every externally distributed artifact, are complete.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are discussing readiness in a cooperative tone and the phrase "signed off" normally signals progress rather than a request for process detail; each silently maps the phrase onto the approval regime they deal with every day.

misalignment_points.topic: Which reserve-rate chart is being reused
misalignment_points.surface_form: They mention reusing "the reserve-rate chart" in the deck and one-pager.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Elena is referring to the updated simulation chart comparing arbitrarily negative reserve rates with a CBDC-based workaround to the cash lower bound, stored in her latest draft folder.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Jason is referring to the earlier chart already shared with design that illustrates why physical cash creates the lower bound under NIRP, from last week's pre-read.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one obviously central chart in the paper's narrative from each person's perspective, and both versions are plausibly described the same way, so the reference feels specific enough even though it is not.

I still expect to tweak prose, chart labels, and probably disclaimer placement right up to release, but that shouldn't hold up design or webinar prep. If we get moving this week, we can land before the client roundtable.
